title: The planetary nebula ESO 378-1
caption: The planetary nebula ESO 378-1, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
celestial: PN K1-22 · constellation Hydra · about 3500 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Ranked #94 on ESO’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: A glowing bubble floats in the darkness of space like the ghost of a star. It may look supernatural, but it is a planetary nebula, the remains of a dying star and a familiar kind of object. This one is cataloged as ESO 378-1, and the picture, captured by ESO's Very Large Telescope in northern Chile, is the best view of this little-known object yet obtained.

Planetary nebulae form near the end of a Sun-like star's life. The star puffs off its outer layers of gas, and the hot, exposed core left behind floods them with energetic light, making them glow. Despite the name, these objects have nothing to do with planets. The term dates back to their round, planet-like look in small telescopes.

The telescope recorded the scene through broad color filters and narrow ones tuned to the glow of oxygen and hydrogen, which trace where these gases shine in the shell. The official caption offers few further details about this particular nebula.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (6.70 x 6.20 arcminutes) and distance (3500 light years), the frame spans roughly 6.8 × 6.3 light-years. Its light set out about 3,500 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was made with the FORS2 instrument on the Very Large Telescope, using B, V and R filters plus filters for oxygen and hydrogen light. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: This faint bubble would be very hard to see by eye. The long exposures on a large telescope bring out its glow.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.

alt: A glowing, ghostly bubble of gas against the dark of space.
